title: Scaling laws, 2020
story:
Before 2020 the question of whether a bigger model would be better was answered by training one. That is an expensive way to hold an opinion, and it made planning impossible: you could not say in advance whether a budget was worth spending, nor how to divide it between a larger model and more data.

Kaplan, McCandlish and colleagues turned it into a measurement. Studying model performance on the cross-entropy loss, they found the loss scales as a power law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude — and that architectural details such as network width or depth have minimal effects within a wide range.

Notice what that second finding does to a field. If the shape of the network barely matters across a wide range, then the cleverness that goes into shaping networks is worth less than the resources poured into them, and the rational move is to stop designing and start scaling. Most of what happened next follows from that sentence.

The paper also gave an allocation rule, and this is the part to watch. Larger models being significantly more sample-efficient, it concluded that optimally compute-efficient training involves training very large models on a relatively modest amount of data, stopping significantly before convergence. The field followed it, and models got very large.

In 2022 Hoffmann and colleagues found that current large language models were significantly undertrained, and said why: a consequence of the recent focus on scaling model size while keeping training data constant. They trained over 400 models, from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters, on 5 to 500 billion tokens, and concluded that for compute-optimal training the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally — double the model, double the data.

Then they tested it in the only way that settles anything. The optimal size for the compute budget of an existing model, Gopher, was predicted to lie between 40 and 70 billion parameters. They trained Chinchilla at 70 billion parameters on 1.4 trillion tokens, for the same number of FLOPs as Gopher's 280 billion parameters, and it uniformly and significantly outperformed Gopher and other larger models across a wide range of downstream tasks, reaching 67.5% average accuracy on the benchmark called MMLU, more than a 7% improvement. Four times smaller, so a smaller memory footprint and a lower inference cost as well.

The interesting question is not who was right. It is how the first result could be sound and its prescription wrong at the same time, because that pattern will show up in your own work.

The answer is that an empirical fit is evidence along the axes you varied, and only those. The first study measured what happens as models grow while the data budget stays roughly where it was, so its conclusion — grow the model — was an honest report of the only direction it had really explored. The second varied both, and found the frontier ran diagonally. Neither study was careless. The difference is which variables were allowed to move, and a curve cannot tell you about a direction nobody travelled.

Take that as the general rule, because it costs nothing and saves a great deal. A measured relationship licenses extrapolation along the axes that moved during the measurement. Anything else is a guess wearing a graph. When someone shows you a scaling curve for a system, the first question is what was held fixed, and the second is whether you are planning to hold it fixed too.

There is a last twist worth carrying, and it is about the question rather than the answer. Both studies optimise the loss you get per unit of training compute. That is not the question a deployed system asks. Training is paid once and serving is paid on every request forever, so the model that is cheapest to reach a given loss is not necessarily the model you want to run — the smaller model's lower inference cost is a point the 2022 paper itself makes. And the same paper notes its analysis runs used less than one epoch of data and that it may still be overestimating the optimal size of large models. Two corrections in a row, each honest about its own limits, is roughly what a healthy empirical field looks like from the inside.

problem.name: Extrapolating from a measured curve
problem.shape: A relationship has been measured over a range, and a decision needs it to hold outside that range.
tell: a budget has to be divided before anything is trained
a curve is being used to justify a direction the experiments never moved in
one variable was held constant throughout and the conclusion is about the others
the metric being optimised is a training cost while the system will pay a serving cost
problem.move: Read which axes moved during the measurement and extrapolate along those only. Before adopting a prescription drawn from a curve, check whether you will hold fixed what the study held fixed, and whether the quantity it optimised is the one you pay.
problem.invariant: A fit is evidence about the region the experiments covered, along the axes they varied — the curve carries no information about a direction nobody travelled.
problem.breaks: Holding a variable constant makes the conclusion conditional on that constant, so a sound measurement can carry an allocation rule that is wrong for anyone who would have varied it.

cost.time: fitting a curve means training many models across sizes and budgets, which is why few groups produce one and many quote it
cost.space: the fit is only as good as its coverage, so the range it spans is part of the result and has to be carried with it
cost.beats: training one model and forming an opinion, which costs as much and generalises to nothing

worked.reasoning:
A scaling law licenses extrapolation along the axes that actually moved while it was measured. Nothing more.

The 2020 result is a genuine one: the loss scales as a power law with model size, dataset size and training compute, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude, and architectural details such as width or depth have minimal effects within a wide range. That second half is why the field turned from designing architectures to scaling them.

Its allocation rule was that larger models are significantly more sample-efficient, so compute-efficient training means very large models on a relatively modest amount of data, stopped significantly before convergence. The field followed it.

The 2022 correction found that models were significantly undertrained, and named the cause: the focus had been on scaling model size while keeping training data constant. Training over 400 models from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens, they concluded model size and training tokens should scale equally — for every doubling of the model, double the tokens.

And they tested it rather than arguing it. For the compute budget of Gopher the optimal size was predicted at 40 to 70 billion parameters; they trained Chinchilla at 70 billion on 1.4 trillion tokens, same FLOPs as Gopher's 280 billion, and it uniformly and significantly outperformed Gopher and larger models, reaching 67.5% on MMLU, more than a 7% improvement, at four times smaller with lower inference cost.

The part I find most useful is how the first result can be sound and its prescription wrong. The first study varied model size with the data budget roughly fixed, so grow the model was an honest report of the only direction explored. The second varied both and found the frontier runs diagonally. A curve says nothing about a direction nobody travelled.

So when I see a scaling curve, the two questions are: what was held fixed, and am I going to hold it fixed too. If not, the curve does not apply to me.

I would add the twist about the question itself. Both studies optimise loss per unit of training compute, and training is paid once while serving is paid on every request. The cheapest model to train to a given loss is not necessarily the one to run, which is why the smaller model's lower inference cost matters — a point the 2022 paper makes itself, alongside noting that its runs used less than one epoch and that it may still be overestimating optimal size.

problem.practice: Find any scaling or benchmark curve in a paper or a blog post and write down, before reading the conclusion, which variables moved and which were held constant. Then read the conclusion and check whether it stays inside that box. Doing this five times will change how you read results permanently.

beats.broke: Whether a bigger model would be better was answered by training one, so a budget could not be planned or divided in advance.
beats.fix: Measure the loss across many sizes and budgets and fit a curve, which turns the question into an extrapolation with a stated shape.
beats.cost: A fit is evidence only along the axes that moved, so the first law's allocation rule was wrong while its shape was right — the data budget had been held roughly constant.

interview.q: What does a scaling law license you to claim, and what was the correction to the first one actually about?
interview.trap: Framing it as one team being wrong. Both measurements were sound; they differed in which variables were allowed to move, and that is the transferable point rather than the scoreline.
interview.answer:
It licenses extrapolation along the axes that moved while it was measured, and nothing else.

The 2020 result is real: loss scales as a power law with model size, dataset size and training compute, some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude, and architectural details like width or depth have minimal effects within a wide range — which is why the field turned from designing architectures to scaling them. Its allocation rule was that larger models are significantly more sample-efficient, so compute-efficient training means very large models on relatively modest data, stopped well before convergence.

The 2022 correction found models were significantly undertrained, because the focus had been on scaling model size while keeping training data constant. Over 400 models from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters, on 5 to 500 billion tokens, gave the rule that model size and tokens should scale equally. They tested it: predicted optimum for Gopher's budget was 40 to 70 billion, they trained Chinchilla at 70 billion on 1.4 trillion tokens at the same FLOPs as Gopher's 280 billion, and it uniformly and significantly outperformed Gopher and larger models — 67.5% on MMLU, more than a 7% improvement, at four times the smaller size and lower inference cost.

What the correction was actually about is the fixed variable. The first study varied model size with the data budget roughly fixed, so its conclusion was an honest report of the only direction it explored; the second varied both and found the frontier runs diagonally. A curve says nothing about a direction nobody travelled.

So my working rule when shown any such curve is to ask what was held fixed and whether I will hold it fixed too. And to notice what is being optimised: both studies minimise loss per unit of training compute, but training is paid once and serving is paid on every request, so the cheapest model to train to a given loss is not necessarily the one to deploy.

takeaway: A scaling law is an empirical fit, so it is evidence only along the axes that moved: the 2020 curve was sound and its advice to grow the model came from holding the data budget roughly fixed, which is why a 70 billion parameter model trained on far more tokens beat a 280 billion one at equal compute — and both optimise training cost, while you pay to serve.
